findings.statement: The online retailer acts as controller of its customers' names, email addresses, postal addresses and order information, since it determines the purposes and means of processing that data for its own retail business.

The attackers' confirmed unauthorized access to the customer database is a personal data breach within the meaning of the GDPR, irrespective of whether the data were downloaded, because unauthorised access to stored personal data alone constitutes such a breach.

As controller, the retailer must notify the breach to the competent supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons; a late notification must be accompanied by reasons for the delay.

The retailer's notification must at least describe the nature of the breach, including the categories and approximate number of affected data subjects and records (here customers' names, email addresses, postal addresses and order data), the contact point for more information, the likely consequences of the breach and the measures taken or proposed to address it; because the retailer does not yet know whether the data were exfiltrated, information not yet available may be provided in phases without undue further delay.

The retailer must document the breach, comprising the facts relating to it, its effects and the remedial action taken, so that the supervisory authority can verify compliance with the notification regime; this documentation duty applies regardless of whether the breach is notified.

The retailer must assess whether the breach is likely to result in a high risk to the affected customers' rights and freedoms; where it is, the retailer must communicate the breach to them without undue delay, in clear and plain language with at least the information and measures referred to in points (b), (c) and (d) of Article 33(3); that communication is not required if any condition in Article 34(3) is met, such as measures applied to the affected data that render them unintelligible to unauthorised persons, and in the disproportionate-effort case a public communication or similar equally effective measure must be made instead.

Following the attack, the retailer must implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including the ability to ensure the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of its processing systems, the ability to restore availability of and access to personal data in a timely manner after an incident, and a process for regularly testing the effectiveness of those measures, account being taken in particular of risks of unauthorised access to personal data.

DORA does not impose obligations on the retailer for this incident, because DORA applies only to the entities listed in Article 2(1), which are the financial entities it collectively designates, and an online retailer is not among them.

The EU AI Act imposes no obligations on the retailer in respect of this breach, because its scope attaches to providers, deployers and other operators of AI systems and general-purpose AI models, and the scenario involves no AI system or model.

summaries.relevance: Supplies the controller definition used to fix the retailer as the actor bearing the notification, communication and documentation duties in this breach.
Establishes the threshold premise of the whole answer: unauthorised access to the customer database is a personal data breach even though exfiltration is unconfirmed.
Creates the primary post-breach duty on the retailer — notification to the supervisory authority within the 72-hour window from awareness unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk.
Fixes the minimum content of the retailer's notification, which it must populate with the known categories of exposed customer data and consequences of the attack.
Permits phased notification, which matters here because the exfiltration question is still open when the 72-hour deadline runs.
Imposes a documentation duty that operates independently of the notification decision and evidences the retailer's handling of the breach to the authority.
Sets the high-risk trigger under which the retailer may additionally owe affected customers direct communication of the breach without undue delay.
Defines what any customer communication must contain, tying its content to the same particulars as the authority notification.
Defines the limited conditions that relieve the retailer of individual communication and the public-communication fallback, bounding the Article 34 duty.
Anchors the retailer's continuing security obligation after the incident, including restoring availability of data and regularly testing its measures.
Directs the security assessment to the very risk materialised here, namely unauthorised access to processed personal data.
Defines the exhaustive list of entities DORA binds, showing an online retailer falls outside its incident-reporting regime for this breach.
Supplies the 'financial entities' collective term that marks out the whole class to which DORA's duties are confined.
Defines who the AI Act reaches — providers, deployers and other operators of AI systems — confirming no AI actor exists in this scenario.

actions: Establish the exact time the retailer became aware of the breach, which starts the 72-hour notification period under Article 33(1).

Settle, in light of the pending investigation into whether data were downloaded, whether the breach is unlikely to result in a risk (Article 33(1)) or likely to result in a high risk to customers requiring communication under Article 34(1).
Identify the supervisory authority competent for the Article 33(1) notification in view of the retailer's establishment(s) and the locations of the affected customers.

Verify whether the retailer operates any AI systems or supplies ICT services to financial entities, which could bring AI Act Article 2(1) or DORA Article 2(1) into play notwithstanding their apparent inapplicability on the facts stated.

Verify whether technical measures such as encryption or pseudonymisation were applied to the affected data, which could satisfy Article 34(3) and remove the duty to communicate individually with customers.
